newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood blames other factions for loss of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Masood blames other factions for loss of Kabul.

text.p: Prominent Afghan guerrilla chief Ahmad Shah Masood on Friday urged the Taleban to cede Kabul to a U.N. force and blamed other factions for letting the turbanned Islamist warriors capture the city in the first place.
"We want the Taleban to evacuate Kabul," Masood, military commander in President Burhanuddin Rabbani's ousted government, told Reuters in the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj.
"A limited international force under U.N. supervision should control Kabul and pave the way for all-party talks on a broad-based government," he said.
Masood, standing in a street giving orders to commanders, made clear the alternative would be war.
"If the Taleban are not ready to cooperate with us, we cannot avoid fighting," he said.

Taleban leaders rejected similar demands from Masood earlier in the week, saying they had enough forces to defend Kabul which they captured on September 27 at the climax of a lightning sweep from the eastern city of Jalalabad.
Masood withdrew his troops and armour from Kabul, chased by the Taleban up to the mouth of his Panjsher Valley lair, losing his Jabal os-Siraj base and the Salang Pass to the north.

He then turned the tables, thrusting down the Salang Pass and out of the Panjsher to drive the Taleban most of the way back to Kabul. But his foes regrouped to prevent him from retaking Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the city.
A devout Moslem himself, Masood has no sympathy for the Taleban's attempts to impose a harsh interpretation of Islamic Sharia law, including sweeping restrictions on women.
His proposal for a peacekeeping force was echoed at the United Nations this week, where other ideas include enforcing a U.N. arms embargo on Afghanistan and demilitarising Kabul.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Thursday that the United States would support an arms ban and described demilitarisation as a useful idea for the future.
But he said it was premature to discuss an international peacekeeping force for the capital.

Masood, known as the "Lion of the Panjsher" for holding the valley against occupying Soviet troops in the 1980s, said he had defended Kabul successfully against all-comers since mujahideen guerrillas took over from a communist government in April 1992.
The Taleban conquered Kabul mainly because neutral and allied forces controlling its eastern approaches had melted away before the black-bearded Pashtun zealots, Masood said.

He focused his fire on Haji Qadir, neutral ex-governor of Nangarhar province, and an old rival, Hezb-i-Islami leader Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who ended his revolt against Rabbani's government to resume his post as prime minister in June.

"Haji Qadir should have defended Jalalabad, but he didn't fight," Masood said. "Hekmatyar, who controlled Sarobi and Laghman, couldn't defend his territory and didn't give government forces a chance to deploy in the right places."

He said the Taleban had exploited these failures to reach the outskirts of the capital. "When our defensive line was broken, we didn't want to fight in Kabul because a lot of civilians would have been killed," Masood added.
Hekmatyar is still allied to Rabbani, but wants a broad-based government, according to a Hekmatyar spokesman.

He has stayed out of a defence pact signed last week by Masood, Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite Moslem faction leader Karim Khalili, and has also taken no part in Pakistani-brokered peace talks between Dostum and the Taleban.

Masood, a Tajik, did not comment on the Dostum-Taleban talks and would not say if troops loyal to Dostum, who staged an abortive attempt to seize Kabul in alliance with Hekmatyar in 1994, had joined in the battle against the Taleban.
Witnesses said Dostum tanks and infantry, pouring down from the Salang Pass at the edge of his territory, had deployed well south of Jabal os-Siraj, but were not yet at the front line.

"In our agreement with Dostum, the most important point is the formation of a broad-based government, which should avoid fighting in Kabul and prepare the ground for peace and elections in Afghanistan," said Masood.
